# The same servers on local Kubernetes

The lab's Postgres images also run as pods on a local cluster, so the pgvector notebook's
concurrency tables can be compared with the compose ones. Every local cluster here is a container
inside Docker Desktop's VM, so this measures Kubernetes networking and pod overhead on the same
cores, not a different machine.

## kind, k3d and k3s

```bash
just k8s-up kind     # stock Kubernetes, ports 5434 / 5435
just k8s-up k3d      # k3s through k3d, ports 5436 / 5437
just k8s-up k3s      # k3s in one container from Python, ports 5438 / 5439
just k8s-test kind   # the pgvector notebook against the cluster
```

| | kind | k3d |
|---|---|---|
| distribution | stock Kubernetes, built with kubeadm | k3s: one binary, SQLite datastore, trimmed components |
| node image | `kindest/node`, 1.3 GB | `rancher/k3s`, about 250 MB |
| cluster create | about 60 s with the image local | about 15 s after the first pull |
| host ports | mapped straight onto the node container | on a separate load-balancer container |
| loading a local image | `kind load docker-image` | `k3d image import` |
| extras by default | none | Traefik ingress and a local-path storage class |

For the benchmark, the choice does not change the result. kind when you want stock Kubernetes,
k3d when you want it fast and small.

## k3s from Python, with no cluster tool at all

Docker Desktop's own Kubernetes is switched on in its settings, and kind's node needs kubeadm run
inside it, so neither can be started from the Docker SDK. k3s can: it is one binary that bootstraps
the whole cluster, which is why k3d is a thin wrapper around the Docker client. `k8s/k3s.py` does
the same with docker-py in about 150 lines:

1. run `rancher/k3s` as a privileged container and wait for the node;
2. stream images in from the local Docker cache (`docker save` into `ctr images import`), so
   nothing is pulled twice;
3. drop the manifests into k3s's auto-deploy directory, which k3s applies on its own, so there is
   no `kubectl` call;
4. wait for the pods and for Postgres to answer on the host port.

About 40 seconds cold, 10 when the container already exists. The pgvector notebook calls it
itself when pointed at `k3s-pg16`, so the Kubernetes run works from a clean machine with only
Docker installed.
